title: Computer-aided molecular design: An introduction and review of tools, applications, and solution techniques
contribution: Tutorial CAMD review: one general optimization program, explicit structural-feasibility constraints for three QSPR families, a four-way taxonomy of solution methods and a tagged table of 73 applications (pp. 11-27).
problem_entry: Chemical product design is presented as trial-and-error over small spaces, against more than 115 million registered structures and about 10^60 drug-like molecules. Two obstacles (no structure-performance map, a space too large to enumerate) are answered by QSPRs. The entry is pedagogical, 'from the ground up', unlike reviews [52, 126] (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: CAMD is the 'reverse problem' of QSPR, written as one program (18)-(25), with single-molecule, mixture and product/process classes as added blocks (pp. 10-14). Feasibility constraints are given per QSPR family (pp. 16-20), solution methods fall into four families (pp. 20-24), and Table 3 is the taxonomy (p. 27).
assumptions: GC is additive in fixed groups, with 'no guarantee' that the groups capture the property (pp. 3-5). TIs are class-restricted (pp. 7-8). SD coloring is subjective, with a risk of overfitting (pp. 8, 10). Nonconvex models need global optimization (p. 12). The Odele-Macchietto balance admits unbuildable sets (p. 16). QSPR error is handled only by re-ranking, and uncertainty is never discussed in the body (pp. 12, 23).
proof_devices: No theorems. Counterexample to a counting rule that is necessary but not sufficient: one >C< and two -Br satisfy (40) at m = 0, and (42) excludes them (p. 16)
Handshaking lemma plus |E| = |V| - 1 + |R| gives the linear degree constraint (57), with coloring-sequence balance (58), parity (59) and a connectivity count (60) (pp. 19-20)
Worked numeric checks of each index and each constraint family on one molecule (Figs. 2-4 and 11-13, pp. 4-8, 17-21)
A process-only relaxation gives a lower bound and ideal targets, and the nearest real molecule gives a feasible point (p. 22)
Deviation variables d+ - d- = pT - p turn target matching into an MILP, (61)-(62) (p. 23); branch-and-bound over underestimators 'linear in many cases' (pp. 22-23)
experiments: None (review). Table 3 tags 73 application papers by QSPR type, method and scope, with no performance numbers (p. 27).
positioning: Builds on the reviews [52, 126] (p. 2). Methods are judged by guarantee, not by results: OA is 'not guaranteed' to be global on nonconvex problems (p. 22), branch-and-bound is global within a tolerance (p. 23). Enumeration suits few descriptors, optimization large or nonconvex spaces (pp. 20, 22). Heuristics are conceded for very large or very nonlinear problems (p. 23), and small heuristic case studies could have been enumerated (p. 25). The group's own papers appear among many (pp. 23, 25-27).
writing: Tutorial register with a figure per concept (Figs. 1-13), paired strengths/weaknesses paragraphs (pp. 5, 7-8, 10), frequent 'we note' asides and a letter-tagged Table 3 (p. 27). Minor slips: typos (pp. 3, 7, 13, 22, 25), duplicate references [68]/[91] (pp. 32-33), a reversed sign in the Fig. 11 label (p. 17).
limits_future: Limits are generic: non-exhaustive coverage (pp. 2, 7), no comparison of methods, QSPR error handled only by re-ranking (p. 12). Future directions are generic too: quantum chemistry, transition-metal catalysts, pharmaceuticals (p. 28).

method_links.note: Algebraic QSPRs make CAMD optimizable ('exact algebraic relationship', p. 12). Product/process design is hard for lack of an algebraic link (p. 14). The group's mixture design keeps derivative-free optimization for a reduced property space ([4] p. 26, [3] p. 25).

Decomposition is framed as step-wise reduction of the design space before costly constraints or models are applied, and Samudra and Sahinidis's three steps follow the same order. The reduction acts on the design space, not on node boxes, and the methods are mostly other people's, as the review frames them.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: screen with the cheap model, re-rank the survivors with higher-order models
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Feasibility problems shrink the candidates to a pool examined with higher-order models or experiments (p. 12). Optimization returns 'the best molecule or a ranking of the top solutions' (Fig. 7, p. 13). Samudra and Sahinidis's step 3 applies 'higher-order models to feasible structures' (p. 23).

Generate-and-test suits few descriptors, optimization large spaces (pp. 20, 22). The small heuristic ionic-liquid case studies 'could thus be alternatively addressed via exhaustive enumeration' (p. 25).

transferable: In an integer model that assembles a molecule or graph from counted blocks, impose both the valence balance (40)/(43) and the inequality that guarantees enough partner groups (42)/(46)-(47); the balance alone admits unbuildable sets (pp. 16-17)
Derive linear feasibility constraints for overlapping descriptors from the handshaking lemma and |E| = |V| - 1 + |R|, plus coloring-sequence balance and parity (57)-(59) (pp. 19-20)

For product/process design, optimize the process with properties as free variables (lower bound and targets), take the nearest real molecule, then re-optimize the process with its properties; report the result as feasible, not global (p. 22)
Make property-target matching an MILP with deviation variables d+ - d- = pT - p (61)-(62) (p. 23)
Before crediting a heuristic's case study, check whether its design space is small enough to enumerate (p. 25)
In a review, tag every application paper by representation, method and scope in one letter-coded table (Table 3, p. 27)
coauthors: Nick D. Austin (Carnegie Mellon University, first author), Daniel W. Trahan (The Dow Chemical Company)

quotes.text: This smaller pool of compounds can then be investigated using high-order models or experiments.
These case studies used a small number of possible groups and could thus be alternatively addressed via exhaustive enumeration.

title: The ALAMO approach to machine learning

coauthors: not read (Scholar lists 'N Sahinidis', per the batch list)

title: The ALAMO approach to machine learning
contribution: Reviews ALAMO (best-subset MIQP, error-maximization sampling, constrained regression) and tests two of its components on 150 synthetic one-input reaction problems, all inside ALAMO (pp. 5-14).
problem_entry: Deep models suit huge data sets but 'can be poorly suited to tasks involving optimization or design' (p. 1). Expensive kinetic data put a premium on simple models, first-principles information and intelligent sampling (p. 2), which become ALAMO's three components. The aim is to review, evaluate and illustrate ALAMO (p. 2).
key_idea: Exact best subset over an explicit basis by a sweep of cardinality-constrained MIQPs (8), or by one convex MIQP (9) for Cp, BIC and RIC (pp. 5-7). Error-maximization sampling by DFO (10) adds points until the maximum error is below delta (pp. 5, 7-8). Constraints on the response over a domain form a semi-infinite program certified by global optimization (p. 8).
assumptions: Linear in parameters over a fixed basis, with inner parameters fixed (p. 5). Normal residuals, with sigma taken from the full OLS fit (pp. 4-5). One response only (p. 5). Big-M = sum |beta_ols| by lasso logic, not argued (p. 7). The relative-error EMS objective divides by z (p. 7). Test data: one input, noise-free closed-form responses (p. 9).
proof_devices: A constant penalty C(r) at fixed cardinality reduces all six fitness metrics to one family of cardinality-constrained MIQPs (pp. 5-7)
Cp, BIC and RIC are convex quadratic in the integer formulation, so one MIQP (9) covers all subsets (pp. 5, 7)
Semi-infinite equivalence: beta is in Omega(chi) iff max_x f <= 0, so a bound certificate is one global maximization (p. 8)
The points EMS adds give a conservative, lower-bound estimate of the maximum error (10) (p. 8)
EF = RMSE_val / RMSE_best (14), and R2_val computed against the training mean, which can be negative (p. 10)
experiments: 150 synthetic problems (2 schemes x 25 rate-constant pairs x 3 species, one input t), a 13-term basis, BIC via (9) and BARON 15.6; no CPU times and no ALAMO version (pp. 9-11). EMS (14-46 points) beats same-size LHS in 120 of 150, but LHS-50 is best in 83 against EMS's 45 (p. 11). Constrained regression wins only below the training range (ECR best in 117 of 150), while UC wins the training and upper domains (pp. 13-14, 19). No external baselines (p. 13).
positioning: Placed within subset selection: exhaustive search is limited (32 regressors), stepwise methods give 'no guarantee of optimality', and the lasso is not best subset (pp. 3-4). The claim that MIP beats the lasso rests on the group's own [17] (p. 4). Concurrent MIP subset-selection work is cited, not compared (p. 3). SNOBFIT is picked from the group's own DFO benchmark [57] (p. 8).
writing: A claims-first experiments section (p. 9) and explicit caveats on unequal comparisons (pp. 11, 13). The abstract and conclusion are stronger than Tables 2-3 (pp. 1, 14 against 12, 19). Count slips: best counts sum to 152/152/155 of 150, 'remaining 36', 147 against 145, and a Table 2 mean above its maximum (pp. 11-14). The printed A model equals B + C (p. 9). Typos (pp. 1, 3, 13, 14).
limits_future: No limitations paragraph and no future work (pp. 13-15). Observed limits: one input, noise-free synthetic data, no external baselines, no timings, no model sizes, no ALAMO version, a basis without the true exponentials, and an unargued big-M (pp. 7-14).

method_links.note: Steps 2-5 are present: a physically motivated basis, an exact MIQP subset with a guaranteed optimal model, certified output bounds that rescue extrapolation below the training range (ECR 117/150), and adversarial sampling that beats same-size LHS in 120/150, with the LHS-50 loss reported. No ALAMO version is named, so the paper is silent on the shipped default (Tension 6).

Step 6 (reading the model) is not practised. The printed A model equals B_ALAMO + C_ALAMO and vanishes at t = 0 where A = 1. Its integer and half-integer power terms have no physical reading, Section 5 never reports model size, and physics enters only as output bounds.
Every compared configuration is an ALAMO option (EMS vs LHS, UC/CR/ECR). BARON 15.6 is named as the engine, and ALAMO is presented as methodology and software.
Step 7: the group's own DFO benchmark [57] chooses the EMS subsolver, SNOBFIT.

The evaluation of their own tool defines metrics and counts losses, but has no hold-out family, no external implementation, no released data and no stated scope. The abstract and conclusion overstate Tables 2-3, which runs against Tension 3's claim that his papers end with losses.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 150 problems from 2 reaction schemes x 25 rate-constant pairs x 3 species, with closed-form responses, validated on 1000 random points each.

transferable: To minimize an information criterion nonlinear in fit and term count (AICc, HQIC, MSE), solve min SSR s.t. sum y_j <= r with big-M links for r = 1..p and keep the best criterion value; criteria linear in the count go into one convex MIQP (pp. 5-7)

Choose the next experiment by maximizing the surrogate's squared relative error with a derivative-free solver; stop when the largest error found is below delta; treat the points found as a lower bound on the true maximum error (pp. 5, 7-8)

Constrain the model's output, not its coefficients, over a domain including outside the training range (bounds, monotonicity or convexity via derivatives), as a semi-infinite constraint certified by globally maximizing the worst violation (p. 8)
Report a sampling method against a space-filling design at the same sample count and against fixed larger budgets, and say which comparisons are unequal (pp. 11, 13)
Score methods by EF = RMSE_val / RMSE_best in a performance profile and report R2_val against the training mean, which exposes models worse than the mean (p. 10)
Make the test library a parametric family of closed-form physical systems (rate constants x schemes x outputs), so ground truth and validation are exact and free (p. 9)
coauthors: Zachary T. Wilson (Carnegie Mellon University, Chemical Engineering, first author)

quotes.text: Although regression-based models should not be used for extrapolation outside of the training domain, enforcing bounds on the response and certifying that a selected model satisfies these bounds can allow for a safer alternative to blind extrapolation.
The astute reader has observed that all sampling schemes compared in this section are implemented in ALAMO.
